summary: This document extends BGP-LS to advertise BGP Peering Segments with their peering node information, so efficient Egress Peer Engineering policies can be computed using Segment Routing. A segment is an instruction, and a list of segment identifiers steers a packet.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC lets a router publish facts about its BGP neighbours over BGP-LS, the protocol used to distribute network topology. Alongside the topology it publishes the segment identifiers, or SIDs, that steer traffic to a particular neighbour, a particular link towards it, or a group of neighbours.

questions: what is bgp egress peer engineering
subtitle: How BGP-LS can carry a router's BGP peering topology and the segment identifiers that steer traffic to those peers.

tldr.problem: A controller that wants to steer traffic out of an autonomous system through one specific BGP neighbour has no standard way to learn what that neighbour looks like or how to address it.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds a BGP-LS Protocol-ID for BGP, two node descriptor TLVs for the BGP router ID and confederation member ASN, and three BGP-LS attribute TLVs carrying the PeerNode, PeerAdj and PeerSet segment identifiers.
tldr.outcome: A router can advertise its BGP peering sessions and the segments that point at them, so a controller can compute egress peer engineering policies. The peering information should stay inside the administrative domain that collected it.

today: RFC 9086 is a Proposed Standard, published in August 2021. No RFC obsoletes it and no RFC updates it, so it is the published definition of these BGP-LS extensions. The companion document RFC 9087 describes the centralized controller solution built on them.

sections.title: Advertising BGP Peering Topology with BGP-LS
sections.content:
Segment Routing (SR) leverages source routing. A node steers a packet through a controlled set of instructions, called segments, by prepending the packet with a list of segment identifiers (SIDs). A SID can represent any instruction, topological or service based. SR segments allow a flow to be enforced through any topological path or service function while maintaining per-flow state only at the ingress node of the SR domain.

The SR architecture (RFC 8402) defines three types of BGP peering segment that may be instantiated at a BGP node. The PeerNode SID is an instruction to steer to a specific peer node. The PeerAdj SID is an instruction to steer over a specific local interface towards a specific peer node. The PeerSet SID is an instruction to load-balance to a set of specific peer nodes. SR can be applied directly to an MPLS data plane, called SR-MPLS, with no change to the forwarding plane, or to a modified IPv6 forwarding plane, called SRv6.

This document describes extensions to the BGP-LS NLRI and the BGP-LS Attribute defined for BGP-LS (RFC 7752), for advertising BGP peering segments from a BGP node along with its peering topology information, meaning its peers, interfaces and peering Autonomous Systems, to enable computation of efficient BGP egress peer engineering policies using the SR-MPLS data plane. The corresponding extensions for SRv6 are specified in a separate Internet-Draft. RFC 9087 illustrates a centralized controller-based solution in which a controller learns the BGP peering SIDs via BGP-LS and then uses them to program an egress peer engineering policy at any node in the domain, so that traffic is steered via a specific BGP egress node to specific external peers, optionally over a specific interface.

The document introduces a new BGP-LS Protocol-ID for BGP and defines new BGP-LS node and link descriptor TLVs, so that BGP-LS link NLRIs can represent the BGP peering topology. It also specifies the BGP-LS attribute TLVs for the three peering segments, to be advertised in the same BGP-LS link NLRI.
sections.plainLanguage: Segment Routing lets the sender list the steps a packet should take. To send traffic out through one chosen BGP neighbour, the sender needs an identifier for that neighbour. This RFC defines how a router publishes that identifier, and the facts about the neighbour, so that a controller elsewhere can use it.

sections.title: The Three BGP Peering Segments
sections.content:
As described in RFC 8402, a BGP-EPE-enabled Egress Provider Edge node instantiates SR segments corresponding to its attached peers. These segments are called BGP peering segments or BGP peering SIDs. In the case of external BGP, they enable the expression of source-routed interdomain paths.

An ingress border router of an AS may compose a list of SIDs to steer a flow along a selected path within the AS, towards a selected egress border router, and to a specific external peer. At minimum, a BGP-EPE policy applied at an ingress node involves two SIDs: the Node SID of the chosen egress node, and then the BGP peering SID for the chosen egress peer's peer or peering interface.

Each BGP session MUST be described by a PeerNode SID, and that description MAY be augmented by additional PeerAdj SIDs. Multiple PeerNode SIDs or PeerAdj SIDs MAY be part of the same group, so that EPE resources can be grouped under a common PeerSet SID. On a router, one PeerNode SID MUST be instantiated for each BGP peer session enabled for egress peer engineering, one or more PeerAdj SIDs MAY be instantiated for the underlying links to the directly connected peer, and a PeerSet SID MAY be instantiated and associated and shared between one or more PeerNode SIDs or PeerAdj SIDs.

While an egress point in a topology usually refers to external BGP sessions between external peers, nothing in these extensions prevents their use with internal BGP sessions. Unlike external sessions, which are generally between directly connected BGP routers also along the traffic forwarding path, internal BGP peer sessions may be set up with BGP routers that are not in the forwarding path. When the internal BGP design includes sessions with route reflectors, a BGP router SHOULD NOT instantiate a BGP peering SID for those sessions, because the purpose of a peering SID is to steer traffic to those specific peers. The applicability for internal BGP peering may therefore be limited to deployments where the peer is also along the forwarding data path.
sections.plainLanguage: Three identifiers cover the useful cases. A PeerNode SID points at a neighbour. A PeerAdj SID points at one particular link towards that neighbour, so you can pick which path leaves the router. A PeerSet SID points at a group of neighbours and lets the traffic be spread across them.

sections.title: The BGP-LS Link NLRI for BGP
sections.content:
The advertisement of BGP peering topology information uses the BGP-LS Link NLRI type, which requires a new BGP-LS Protocol-ID. The Protocol-ID 7 is used, with the NLRI information source protocol being BGP. Using a new Protocol-ID allows the BGP-LS NLRIs carrying BGP information to be separated and differentiated from those carrying IGP link-state information defined in RFC 7752. The BGP peering information, along with the peering segments, is advertised using the BGP-LS Link NLRI type with that Protocol-ID, using the descriptor TLVs and BGP-LS attribute TLVs as defined in RFC 7752.

Two new node descriptor TLVs are defined. The BGP Router Identifier has type 516, length 4 octets, and a value that is a 4-octet unsigned non-zero integer representing the BGP Identifier as defined in RFC 6286. The Member-AS Number has type 517, length 4 octets, and a value that is a 4-octet unsigned non-zero integer representing the Member-AS Number of RFC 5065.

When distributing BGP information, the BGP Router-ID (TLV 516) and the Autonomous System Number (TLV 512) MUST be included as local node descriptors, describing the local BGP node. The same two TLVs MUST be included as remote node descriptors, describing the peer BGP node. The ASN carries the AS number, or the AS Confederation Identifier if confederations are used. Section 2.1 of RFC 6286 requires the BGP identifier to be unique within an Autonomous System and non-zero, so the pair of ASN and BGP router ID is globally unique, and using it in the node descriptor helps map link-state NLRIs with the BGP protocol ID to a unique BGP router in the administrative domain where BGP-LS is enabled.

The Member-ASN (TLV 517) MAY be included as a local or remote node descriptor when BGP confederations are used, as may the node descriptors defined in RFC 7752.
sections.plainLanguage: The advertisement is a standard BGP-LS link record with a new protocol number, 7, so that consumers can tell BGP peering facts apart from ordinary link-state facts. Two new fields identify a router: its BGP router ID and its AS number. A third, the member AS number, is only needed when the AS uses confederations.

sections.title: The Peering SID TLVs
sections.content:
Three new BGP-LS link attribute TLVs are defined for advertising BGP peering SIDs: type 1101 for the PeerNode SID, 1102 for the PeerAdj SID and 1103 for the PeerSet SID. All three have the same format. The Type field carries the code point, and the Length field is variable, with valid values of either 7 or 8 octets depending on whether the encoding is done as a SID index or as a label. A one-octet Flags field carries four flags and four reserved bits. The V-Flag, the value flag, means the SID carries a label value, and is set by default. The L-Flag, the local flag, means the value or index carried by the SID has local significance, and is also set by default. The B-Flag, the backup flag, means the SID refers to a path that is eligible for protection using fast reroute. The P-Flag, the persistent flag, means the SID is persistently allocated, so the SID value remains consistent across a router restart and a session or interface flap. The reserved bits must be zero when originated and ignored when received.

A one-octet Weight field carries the weight of the SID for the purpose of load balancing. The SID, index or label field contains either a 3-octet local label where the 20 rightmost bits are used for the label value, in which case the V and L flags must be set, or a 4-octet index defining the offset in the Segment Routing Global Block advertised by this router, in which case the SRGB must be advertised using the extensions defined in RFC 9085. The values of the PeerNode, PeerAdj and PeerSet SID sub-TLVs SHOULD be persistent across a router restart.

When egress peer engineering is enabled, the router MUST include the PeerNode SID TLV in the BGP-LS attribute for the BGP-LS link NLRI corresponding to its BGP peering sessions. The PeerAdj SID and PeerSet SID TLVs MAY be included. Additional BGP-LS link attribute TLVs defined in RFC 7752 MAY be included, for example the interface addresses of the underlying link or links over which a multi-hop BGP peering session is set up.

The PeerNode SID has the SR operation NEXT, with the connected peering node to which the segment is associated as next hop. It is advertised in an NLRI whose link descriptors include the IPv4 interface address (TLV 259) and IPv4 neighbour address (TLV 260), and the IPv6 interface address (TLV 261) and IPv6 neighbour address (TLV 262), holding the addresses used by the BGP session. The PeerAdj SID also has the SR operation NEXT, with the interface peer address as next hop. Its link descriptors MUST include the Link Local/Remote Identifiers (TLV 258), holding the 4-octet link local identifier followed by the 4-octet link remote identifier, with the value 0 used by default when the remote identifier is unknown. The PeerSet SID also has the SR operation NEXT, with load-balancing across any connected interface to any peer in the associated peer set as next hop. The PeerSet SID TLV containing the same SID value is included in the BGP-LS attribute for all the link NLRIs corresponding to the PeerNode or PeerAdj segments associated with the peer set.
sections.plainLanguage: Each peering segment travels in its own attribute field, and the three fields have the same shape: a flags byte, a weight byte for load balancing, and the identifier itself, either as a label or as an offset into a block of identifiers the router has advertised. The flags say whether the identifier is a label, whether it is only meaningful on this router, whether it has a backup path, and whether it survives a restart.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The document defines one new Protocol-ID in the BGP-LS Protocol-IDs registry, the value 7 for BGP, which identifies BGP as the source protocol of the NLRI information.

It also defines five new TLVs, all in the registry for BGP-LS node descriptor, link descriptor, prefix descriptor and attribute TLVs. Two are node descriptor TLVs: type 516, BGP Router-ID, and type 517, BGP Confederation Member. Three are link attribute TLVs: type 1101, PeerNode SID, type 1102, PeerAdj SID, and type 1103, PeerSet SID.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC registers one new protocol number, 7, and five new code points: two for describing a BGP router and three for carrying the peering segments.

sections.title: Manageability Considerations
sections.content:
The new protocol extensions augment the existing IGP topology information distributed by BGP-LS by adding support for distributing BGP peering topology information, so the manageability considerations in Section 6 of RFC 7752 apply to them as well. In particular, the malformed link-state NLRI and BGP-LS attribute tests for syntactic checks now apply to the TLVs defined here. The semantic or content checking for those TLVs and their association with the BGP-LS NLRI types or BGP-LS attributes is left to the consumer of the BGP-LS information, such as an application or a controller, and not to the BGP protocol.

A consumer retrieves this information from a BGP speaker over a BGP-LS session. How it handles semantic or content errors depends on its application and is beyond the scope of the document. An error detected in the NLRI descriptor TLVs would be expected to make that specific NLRI update unusable, so the update is discarded along with an error log, whereas an error in attribute TLVs would result in only that specific attribute being discarded with an error log.

The operator MUST be provided with the options of configuring, enabling and disabling the advertisement of each of the PeerNode SID, PeerAdj SID and PeerSet SID, as well as control of which information is advertised to which internal or external peer. BGP peering segments are associated with the normal BGP routing peering sessions, but the peering information and the segments themselves are advertised over a distinct BGP-LS peering session, and it is expected that this isolation is followed when advertising BGP peering topology information via BGP-LS.

Egress peer engineering enables the instantiation of a segment routing path for traffic engineering a flow via an egress BGP router to a specific peer, bypassing the normal BGP best-path routing for that flow and any routing policies implemented in BGP on that egress router. As with any traffic-engineering solution, the controller or application implementing the policy needs to ensure that there is no looping or misrouting of traffic. Traffic counters corresponding to the MPLS label of the peering SID on the router would indicate the traffic being forwarded based on the specific EPE path, and monitoring those counters and the flows hitting the corresponding MPLS forwarding entry would help identify issues.
sections.plainLanguage: An operator has to be able to switch each kind of peering segment on or off and to choose which peers receive them, because the peering facts reveal how the network is connected to the outside. The controller that computes policies has to avoid creating loops, and the routers need counters so the operator can see how much traffic each policy is actually carrying.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
RFC 7752 defines the BGP-LS NLRI to which these extensions apply, and Section 8 of RFC 7752 also applies to them. The procedures and new TLVs defined here, by themselves, do not affect the BGP-LS security model discussed in RFC 7752.

BGP-EPE enables engineering of traffic when leaving the administrative domain via an egress BGP router, so precaution is necessary to ensure that the BGP peering information collected via BGP-LS is limited to specific consumers in a secure manner. Segment Routing operates within a trusted domain, and its security considerations also apply to BGP peering segments. The BGP-EPE policies are expected to be used entirely within this trusted SR domain, for example between multiple ASes or domains within a single provider network.

The isolation of BGP-LS peering sessions is also required, so that the BGP-LS topology information, including the newly added BGP peering topology, is not advertised to an external BGP peering session outside an administrative domain.
sections.plainLanguage: The peering facts describe how the network connects to other networks, so they should not leak outside the domain that collects them. The BGP-LS session that carries them must be kept separate from the sessions that talk to external peers.
